citation: Timofey Sanko, Yuan Tian, Mariam Guizani (Queen's University, Kingston, Ontario). 'BurnRiSc: Toward Non-Invasive Burnout Screening in Open Source from Public Repository Signals'. arXiv:2609.19422v1 [cs.CY], 16 September 2026. Submitted to Journal Ahead Workshop (JAWs '26), Munich. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19422 ; code: https://github.com/RISElabQueens/BurnRiSc. Note: the arXiv page says 8 pages; the PDF's ACM reference line says 10 pages.

exact_quotes: Abstract: "sustained BRS elevation precedes 6 of 10 disclosures by 6-15 months, 8 of 10 when adding peak BRS as a second criterion, and 10 of 10 over any prior time frame. We thus present BurnRiSc as evidence that burnout is screenable from public data."
Abstract: "In a preliminary evaluation across 68 contributors in ten repositories (ten disclosed burnout cases, twelve comparable-volume collapses, and 46 comparison contributors)"

Abstract: "operationalizes the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory's two dimensions, exhaustion and disengagement, as 14 behavioral and linguistic signals computed from GitHub activity and scored against each contributor's own history."
Sec 3.2: "The BRS is not a diagnosis: it signals that a contributor may benefit from being checked in on and offered support."
Sec 5.1: "Among the 46 comparison contributors, 35 (76.08%) never cross the threshold. The remaining 11 cannot be treated as errors outright."
Sec 5.1: "We regard roughly one crossing in five as reasonable, given that OSS contribution patterns are highly irregular"
Sec 5.2: "The resulting risk threshold, derived from the Equal-anchored fit's peak distribution, is 0.412"
Sec 5.2: "Leave-one-out-cross-validation ... finds 7 of 10 confirmed cases still rank above this floor when held out."
Sec 5.3: "Peak BRS correlates weakly with activity score (r = 0.260, r2 = 0.068, p = 0.032)"

Sec 5.3: "16 out of the 27 contributors with a peak risk above the threshold turn out to be either confirmed cases or highly-ranked activity collapse cases ... so 16/27 is a lower bound on precision."
Sec 6: "BurnRiSc is a screening tool, not a diagnostic tool."
Sec 6: "A high BurnRiSc score should prompt concern, not a conclusion."
Sec 6: "This framework should not trigger an evaluation initiated by someone else."

Sec 6: "if contributors' behavior affects their standing, they may mask the very signals that BurnRiSc depends on, defeating its purpose and denying them the support it was designed to surface. The goal of the framework is to identify people who need support, not to penalize them for needing it."
Sec 6 (future plans): "ten confirmed cases suffice to demonstrate feasibility but not to fit fourteen weights or support robust statistics"
Sec 6 (future plans): "this evaluation validates BRS against disclosure timing rather than against OLBI scores directly administered to the same individuals."

Sec 6 (ethics, final sentence of future plans): "Finally, we plan to develop the ethical framing this paper sketches, because inferring psychological state from public traces raises questions of consent and appropriate use."
Sec 4.2: "We withhold names and handles to avoid re-identifying the disclosers."
date_and_recency: Published 16 September 2026 (arXiv v1). Disclosure dates in Table 2 run from Dec 2016 to Dec 2025; GitHub activity histories go back to at least 2011. Peak BRS month for Dev 8 is listed as June 2026. Very recent, unreplicated.
key_claims: Burnout, as operationalised by the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (OLBI) dimensions exhaustion and disengagement, can be approximated from public GitHub traces (timestamps, throughput, commit/PR/issue text).

A monthly Burnout Risk Score (BRS, 0 to 1) is the mean of an exhaustion score and a disengagement score; each signal is scored against the contributor's own history (level percentile plus 4-month trend percentile, smoothed, passed through a sigmoid).
Sustained BRS elevation precedes publicly disclosed burnout in a majority of ten cases, with a lead time of months.
BRS is not just a proxy for how active a contributor is (weak correlation with an independent activity score).
Off-hours activity and commit volume carry the most weight after fitting.
The authors call it a screening tool and not a diagnosis; a flag should prompt a cheap, non-judgmental check-in.
headline_figures: 14 signals: 7 exhaustion proxies (Off-hours Activity, Linguistic Arousal, PR Merge Time, Lexical Exhaustion, Sentiment-Exhaustion, Lexical Diversity, Hapax Rate) and 7 disengagement proxies (Commit Volume, Review Participation, PR Rejection Rate, Task Abandonment, Pronoun Use, Lexical Disengagement, Sentiment-Disengagement). Source: Table 1.

68 contributors across ten GitHub repositories (Sec 4.2). Selection: ten most prolific by commit count per repository plus any discloser outside that set (100 candidates), then filtered to humans (no [bot]) with at least three years of history. Made up of 10 confirmed disclosed-burnout cases, 12 activity-collapse cases (weakly labelled, not burnout cases) and 46 comparison contributors.

6 of 10 confirmed cases flagged by sustained onset (BRS above threshold for the first month plus at least two further consecutive months) within the 24-month lookback, at lead times of 6 to 15 months (Sec 5.1).
8 of 10 when lifetime peak BRS above threshold within the window is admitted as a second criterion, at lead times of 5 to 16 months. The two outside the two-year window are Dev 5 and Dev 8.

10 of 10 'over any prior time frame' (abstract); the Introduction says every disclosure is preceded by at least one elevated period outside the 24-month window. Table 2 lead times include 40, 52 and 61 months, so this is a very loose criterion.
Activity-collapse cases (12): 6 flagged 4 to 13 months before the biggest decline; 10 of 12 with peak BRS as a secondary criterion.
Comparison group: 11 of 46 crossed the threshold (onset or threshold-crossing peak at any point); 35 of 46 (76.08%) never did. Authors call about one in five 'reasonable'. 11/46 is 23.9%.

Risk threshold 0.412: midpoint between the comparison group's 75th percentile and the activity-collapse group's 25th percentile of peak BRS, from the Equal-anchored fit. Chosen so that confirmed cases are caught, so it deliberately trades more false positives for fewer false negatives.
Separation margin: unweighted baseline 0.121; fitted Equal 0.243, Exhaustion-heavy 0.241, Disengagement-heavy 0.224, Heuristic 0.187. Bootstrap (100 resamples): mean 0.215, std 0.008.

Leave-one-out cross-validation over the ten confirmed cases: 7 of 10 still rank above the 80th percentile of the training comparison-group peak distribution when held out. So 3 of 10 are missed out of sample.

Peak BRS vs independent activity score: r = 0.260, r2 = 0.068, p = 0.032 (Sec 5.3). The paper says 'real, statistically detectable association ... accounting for a low amount of the variance'. Only four contributors fall in the 'over-analysis risk' quadrant (low activity, high risk).

27 contributors had peak BRS above the threshold; 16 of 27 were confirmed cases or highly ranked collapse cases (lower bound on precision about 59%; the other 11 are unlabelled, not shown to be errors).
Top fitted weights averaged across anchors: Off-hours Activity 2.668, Commit Volume 2.416, Lexical Exhaustion 1.324. Lowest: Review Participation 0.092, Rejection Rate 0.089.

Sentiment classifier: fine-tuned RoBERTa, macro-F1 0.889 (10-fold CV) vs 0.870 for the original BERT on the Biswas et al. dataset. Lexical-feature check: 67.78% of high-similarity messages judged genuine matches in a 90-message manual review (sarcasm the main false-positive source).

Repo vs paper discrepancy: the GitHub README (as rendered) lists nine signals and a default RISK_THRESHOLD of 0.305, not 14 signals and 0.412. Treat the paper as the source of record; the repo may be an earlier or reduced version [uncertain].
sample_unit_and_population: Unit: individual GitHub contributor within a repository. 68 contributors in ten repositories, all long-tenured core contributors (top ten by commits, at least three years of history, human accounts). Only ten repositories were chosen because each contained a public burnout discloser. Repositories are anonymised ('identified by number') and names and handles are withheld, so the cases cannot be independently checked. These are open-source maintainers, not employed software teams. Disclosure dates span 2016 to 2025.
observed_vs_stated: Mixed. The inputs are observed behaviour (timestamps, commit counts, PR outcomes, message text). The outcome label for the ten cases is a self-stated public disclosure found by keyword search (tired, burntout, burnout, leaving) and manually verified. The burnout date is set to the month of the disclosure post. No OLBI or MBI questionnaire was administered to anyone, so the score is not validated against a measured burnout state.
what_it_measures_or_defines: Burnout is defined via WHO (chronic occupational syndrome from unmanaged workplace stress) and the Job Demands-Resources model. The instrument approximated is the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory: exhaustion and disengagement. BRS = (E + D) / 2, a 0 to 1 monthly relative risk score per person, indexed to their own history. It is a proxy for behavioural and linguistic change, not a measure of burnout itself. Authors state it 'is not a diagnosis'.
mechanism_or_cause: Job Demands-Resources theory: sustained demands unmatched by available resources. The authors argue open source is close to a worst case: maintainers absorb unbounded demand from users who bear no cost, with no manager to reallocate work, no organisation to notice decline and no compensation. This is asserted from the literature, not tested in the study.
interventions_and_effects: No intervention was tested. The paper recommends pairing any flag with 'a cheap, non-judgmental response', a prompt for the contributor to reflect and, if warranted, take a break, and says it must not trigger an evaluation initiated by someone else. It lists questions for future work (whether risk falls after joining a foundation, securing funding, adding maintainers, or adopting AI coding agents) but reports no effect sizes.
transfer_to_software_teams: Evidence is from ten open-source repositories and long-tenured core contributors only, with GitHub-visible activity. Transfer to employed teams is untested: signals like off-hours activity, commit volume and PR merge time depend heavily on local norms, and the paper itself notes review-heavy organisations might weight signals differently. The authors note that peripheral contributors, newcomers and people who burn out silently are outside what has been tested. Plausible as a research idea for teams; not evidence that it works there.
limitations_stated: "ten confirmed cases suffice to demonstrate feasibility but not to fit fourteen weights or support robust statistics" (Sec 6). Weights and threshold are fit on the same small set.

Confirmed cases are disclosers only: "they may differ systematically from those who experience burnout silently". Transfer to silent cases is untested; the activity-collapse group is only a weakly labelled hedge.
Keyword-based disclosure detection "missing indirect, off-platform, and non-English disclosures".
Three-year tenure rule and top-ten-by-commit selection restrict the study to established core contributors.
Validated against disclosure timing, not against OLBI scores administered to the same people.
Burnout date is the disclosure month, which is conservative since burnout may have preceded disclosure.
The comparison group reflects absence of disclosure, not absence of burnout, so the 11 crossings may include undisclosed true positives; precision is called a lower bound.
Low weights for review participation and rejection rate may reflect thin data rather than no signal.

Text signals assume a human author; commits and comments written with language models, or AI agents sustaining commit volume while the person disengages, could distort them. Direction of bias unclear.
Threshold and onset definitions are 'decisions about how to read its output' and were set after seeing the data; threshold derived from the fitted weights and should be re-evaluated on larger data.

Ethics: the paper only sketches it. Authors say they plan to develop the ethical framing because 'inferring psychological state from public traces raises questions of consent and appropriate use.' They also warn that using scores to evaluate people would lead to masking of signals. No ethics board or consent process is described for the ten disclosers or the other 58 people; names withheld to avoid re-identification.
counter_evidence: Internal: (1) Out-of-sample, leave-one-out catches only 7 of 10. (2) The 6 of 10 headline needs an onset within 24 months; the 10 of 10 figure counts any elevated period at any earlier time, with lead times up to 61 months, which is weak evidence of prediction. (3) The threshold was set at the midpoint between comparison and collapse groups after seeing the data, and the 8 of 10 uses a second criterion added to recover missed cases. (4) 11 of 46 comparison contributors (about 24%) cross the threshold, and 27 people in total exceed it, of whom only 16 are known cases or collapse cases. (5) Table 2 shows two confirmed cases (Dev 3 and Dev 6) with no flag at all and Dev 4 has a peak 'N/A'; several flags are long before disclosure. (6) r = 0.26 with p = 0.032 is a weak but real association with activity, and the activity-collapse group is itself defined by activity drops, which overlaps with the commit-volume signal that carries high weight, so some circularity is possible [uncertain, my reading]. (7) Weights and signal selection were fit on the same ten cases being evaluated, aside from leave-one-out. External: the paper cites Ehsani et al. and Mäntylä et al. as showing affect, not burnout, is what repository studies capture; no independent replication yet. Repo README shows nine signals and threshold 0.305, so published artefacts do not obviously match the paper.

usable_claim: A preprint workshop paper (Sanko, Tian and Guizani, September 2026) turned the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory into 14 signals taken from public GitHub activity and tested them on 68 contributors in ten open-source repositories. In its ten publicly disclosed burnout cases, a sustained rise in the score came 6 to 15 months before the disclosure in 6 cases, and in 8 when a one-month peak was also allowed. About one in four comparison contributors (11 of 46) also crossed the threshold. The authors call it a screening idea, not a diagnosis, say ten cases is too few to fit the weights, and say a flag should lead to a gentle check-in and never an evaluation by someone else.
do_not_use: Do not say it 'predicts' burnout or that burnout is 'screenable from public data' as settled (that is the authors' framing in a preliminary workshop paper). Do not use the '10 of 10' figure. Do not call the 6/8 of 10 an accuracy or imply it holds out of sample (leave-one-out is 7 of 10). Do not drop the 11 of 46 false-alarm figure. Do not present the 12 collapse cases as burnout cases. Do not use 0.412 as a usable cut-off, or r = 0.26 as 'no relation to activity' (it is a weak but significant correlation, p = 0.032). Do not apply it to employed software teams or suggest managers could run it; the paper explicitly says it must not trigger an evaluation initiated by someone else. Do not use the repo's nine-signal or 0.305 defaults. Do not claim a validated link to OLBI scores; none were collected.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the text of 'Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part', the trust essay or 'Checking Isn't Catching' by this agent (essays not opened). Based on the commit history these deal with agent oversight and trust, so likely no overlap, though the paper's AI-mediated-contribution caveat (agents can keep commit volume up while a person disengages) touches the same ground.
